summary: A 1970 paper on systems for interprocess communication in a resource-sharing computer network, by D. C. Walden. It replaces RFC 61 and looks at how programs on separate computers can communicate.

plainLanguage.summary: This note describes ways for programs on different computers to talk to each other, and replaces an earlier draft.

questions: what is a rendezvous site in early arpanet ipc
subtitle: A 1970 proposal for process-to-process messaging with SEND and RECEIVE, ports and a rendezvous site.

tldr.problem: In a resource sharing network, resources belong to processes, so sharing them is a problem of letting processes talk to each other, locally and across computers.
tldr.mechanism: Six monitor operations (SEND, RECEIVE, SEND FROM ANY, RECEIVE ANY, SLEEP, UNIQUE) move messages between numbered ports. For remote processes, a distributed Network Controller matches SENDs and RECEIVEs in a rendezvous table at a rendezvous site.
tldr.outcome: The author says it has not been implemented and is a personal view, not an official BBN position. He suggests the ARPA Network consider placing these operations in the IMP.

facts.label: Operations
facts.value: SEND, RECEIVE, SEND FROM ANY, RECEIVE ANY, SLEEP, UNIQUE

today: The metadata lists no standards status for RFC 62. It supersedes RFC 61, and the text describes itself as an unimplemented personal proposal, not an official BBN position.

sections.title: Introduction and Goal
sections.content:
D. C. Walden of BBN supersedes RFC 61 here. He defines a resource sharing computer network as autonomous computer systems interconnected so each can use the resources of the others much as it would call a subroutine.

He views resources as belonging to processes, so he treats interprocess communication as the fundamental problem. The study has two parts: a set of operations for one time-sharing system that avoids tricks like shared memory, and a generalization to remote processes. The paper stresses that it is not an official BBN position on Host protocol for the ARPA Computer Network.
sections.plainLanguage: If programs on different computers are going to help each other, the first thing they need is a way to pass notes.

sections.title: Six Operations Inside One System
sections.content:
In a model time-sharing system, processes ask the monitor for six operations. RECEIVE and SEND each take a RECEIVE port, a SEND port, a buffer and a restart location. RECEIVE ANY accepts a message from any process. SEND FROM ANY sends to such a process. SLEEP waits for an event. UNIQUE returns a unique number from the monitor.

A port is a data path with a unique port number. If process A does a RECEIVE to port N from port M and process B does a SEND to port N from port M, the monitor matches the numbers and moves the message. Nothing happens until both sides have been executed, so no data starts flowing before a RECEIVE, which gives flow control. Unmatched entries time out and the process is notified, and a RECEIVE ANY never times out.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender and a receiver each write down the same pair of mailbox numbers. When the monitor sees both, it passes the message along.

sections.title: Extending It Across a Network
sections.content:
The design generalizes by letting a Network Controller perform the operations. In a star network it sits at the centre. In a network with no centre its functions are spread over the sites. Each site then keeps a rendezvous table of unmatched SENDs and RECEIVEs, and each site is given a portion of the unique numbers.

A RECEIVE names a rendezvous site, normally the SEND site. The RECEIVE message travels there, the matching SEND meets it, and the transmission goes to the site that sent the RECEIVE. A RECEIVE ANY never leaves its own site, which is why SEND FROM ANY exists: it is sent at once and discarded if no receiver exists. The paper shows how a RECEIVE port or a SEND port can move to another site, and offers three ways to manage unique numbers, one of which suggests numbers of about 32 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Each town keeps a meeting board. The sender's and receiver's requests meet there, and then the message is sent on to wherever the receiver is.

sections.title: Application to the ARPA Network and Conclusion
sections.content:
The paper describes the ARPA Network of the time as ten sites, each with one to three (potentially four) Hosts and one IMP, joined by 50-kilobit phone lines. The author proposes that the IMPs provide SEND, RECEIVE, SEND FROM ANY, RECEIVE ANY and UNIQUE, so the Host/Host protocol program is written once rather than many times. Pieces of one buffer could then travel in parallel network messages with several RFNMs outstanding.

He states that the system has not been implemented, so he has no performance reports. His four conclusions are openly subjective. He calls the system under development for ARPA a step in the wrong direction and suggests his method be considered for adoption.
sections.plainLanguage: The author thinks the network's message-moving boxes should do the matching work, so each computer does not have to redo it, and he admits he has not built it yet.
